title: Point at Issue and Point of Agreement
summary: Two speakers. For disagreement, find a claim one affirms and the other denies; for agreement, one both commit to. Use the two-speaker check on every choice.

slides.title: Both speakers must have a view
body: The right answer to a disagreement question is a claim on which both speakers take a position, and the positions are opposite.
Most wrong answers fail because one speaker says nothing about the claim. A topic only one person addresses can’t be a point of disagreement, or of agreement.
slides.callout: For each choice: what would speaker 1 say? What would speaker 2 say? You need two answers, and for disagreement they must clash.

slides.title: How you’ll see it
stems: Lena and Omar disagree over whether…
The dialogue provides the most support for the claim that the two disagree over whether…
Their statements indicate that they would be most likely to agree that…
The exchange most strongly supports the claim that both speakers would accept which one of the following?

steps.label: Speaker one’s claim
steps.do: What is the first speaker’s conclusion?

steps.label: Speaker two’s response
steps.do: What does the second speaker reject, and what does she concede? Concessions are agreement points.

steps.label: Predict
steps.do: Disagreement is usually over speaker one’s conclusion or a premise speaker two attacks.

steps.label: Two-speaker check
steps.do: For every choice, write a yes, no or silent for each speaker. Keep only yes/no pairs (or yes/yes for agreement).

slides.title: Level 1: a plain yes against a no
slides.stimulus:
Greta: The town library should open on Sundays. Many families can visit only on weekends, and Saturday hours are not enough for them.
Pavel: Sunday hours would cost more than the library can afford. The town would do better to spend that money on new books.
slides.stem: Greta and Pavel disagree over whether

choices.A: many families can visit the library only on weekends
choices.B: the town library should open on Sundays
choices.C: the library's collection needs new books
choices.D: Saturday hours are long enough for most families
choices.E: the library's staff are willing to work on Sundays

steps.label: Greta's claim
steps.note: The library should open on Sundays. Her reason is that families need weekend time.
steps.highlight: The town library should open on Sundays.

steps.label: Pavel's response
steps.note: He says Sunday hours cost too much and the money should go elsewhere. So he says no to Sunday opening.
steps.highlight: Sunday hours would cost more than the library can afford.

steps.label: Two-speaker check
steps.note: Open Sundays? Greta yes, Pavel no. That is the clash. A and C are claims only one speaker makes; D is Greta's alone; E is neither's.

why.A: Pavel never speaks to weekend visits. Only Greta takes a position.
why.B: Correct. Greta says yes; Pavel's objection to Sunday hours says no.
why.C: Only Pavel mentions new books. Greta is silent.
why.D: Greta says Saturday is not enough for those families. Pavel says nothing about Saturday.

slides.title: Level 2: the method, step by step
slides.stimulus:
Lena: The city should ban cars from Main Street on weekends. Shops on pedestrian streets in other cities saw their sales rise.
Omar: Those cities have large tourist populations, which Main Street lacks. A weekend ban here would more likely hurt the shops' sales by keeping out shoppers who drive in from the suburbs.
slides.stem: Lena and Omar disagree over whether

choices.A: shops on pedestrian streets in other cities saw their sales rise
choices.B: Main Street draws large numbers of tourists
choices.C: a weekend car ban on Main Street would help the sales of its shops
choices.D: suburban shoppers prefer shopping on pedestrian streets
choices.E: the city should consider other ways to increase sales on Main Street

steps.label: Lena
steps.note: Ban cars; the evidence implies sales would rise here.
steps.highlight: Shops on pedestrian streets in other cities saw their sales rise.

steps.label: Omar
steps.note: Doesn't dispute the other cities. Says a ban here would hurt sales.
steps.highlight: would more likely hurt the shops' sales

steps.label: Two-speaker check
steps.note: Would the ban help Main Street’s sales? Lena: yes. Omar: no. That’s the clash. Notice A is something they both accept: it would answer an agreement question.

why.A: Omar doesn't dispute it. On an agreement question, this would be the answer.
why.B: Lena says nothing about tourists on Main Street.
why.C: Correct. Lena implies the ban would raise sales; Omar says it would hurt them.
why.D: Neither speaker discusses suburban shoppers' preferences.

slides.title: Level 3: the clash is hidden inside a rejected test
slides.stimulus:
Hollis: The museum's decision to charge admission has been a failure. Attendance fell by a fifth in the first year, and an institution that exists to educate the public should not put barriers in the public's way.
Ravi: Counting heads is the wrong test. Before the fee, many visitors came in only to get out of the rain and left within minutes. The fee now pays for the new education wing, and the number of school groups visiting has doubled.
slides.stem: Hollis and Ravi disagree over whether

choices.A: attendance at the museum fell during the first year after the fee was introduced
choices.B: an institution that exists to educate the public should avoid putting barriers in the public's way
choices.C: the number of school groups visiting the museum has increased since the fee began
choices.D: many visitors before the fee came in only to get out of the rain
choices.E: the drop in attendance shows that the fee has been a failure

steps.label: Hollis's claim
steps.note: The fee is a failure, and his evidence is the fall in attendance.
steps.highlight: The museum's decision to charge admission has been a failure.

steps.label: Ravi's response
steps.note: He never says 'the fee is a success'. He rejects the test: counting heads is wrong. He does not deny that attendance fell.
steps.highlight: Counting heads is the wrong test.

steps.label: Predict the clash
steps.note: The clash sits in Hollis's inference, from the fall in attendance to failure. Ravi rejects that step.

steps.label: Two-speaker check
steps.note: A: Hollis states, Ravi does not deny. B: Hollis only. C and D: Ravi only. E: Hollis yes, Ravi no. The hard part is that Ravi's 'no' is implied by his attack on the test.

why.A: Ravi does not dispute the fall; his point is that it does not matter. No clash.
why.B: Only Hollis says this. Ravi takes no position on barriers.
why.C: Only Ravi gives this fact. Hollis is silent.
why.D: Only Ravi says this. Hollis does not discuss why visitors came.
why.E: Correct. Hollis says the fall shows failure; Ravi says attendance is the wrong test, so it shows no such thing.

slides.title: Level 4: agreement hidden in a concession
slides.stimulus:
Imani: When a company's board approves a merger, shareholders who opposed it should be allowed to sell their shares back to the company at the pre-announcement price. Without that right, a majority can impose losses on a minority, and a minority has no other way out.
Dov: A buyback right would let any unhappy shareholder demand payment after a vote, and boards would become afraid to propose mergers, even beneficial ones. A minority can certainly be harmed by a majority's decision, but harm of that kind is an ordinary risk of owning shares, and the law already protects minorities against fraud.
slides.stem: The exchange most strongly supports the claim that both speakers would accept which one of the following?

choices.A: a buyback right at the pre-announcement price would discourage boards from proposing beneficial mergers
choices.B: a minority of shareholders will suffer losses whenever a majority approves a merger
choices.C: a minority of shareholders can suffer losses because a majority approved a merger
choices.D: minority shareholders already have enough legal protection against losses from mergers
choices.E: shareholders who oppose an approved merger should be able to sell their shares back at the pre-announcement price

steps.label: Imani's claim
steps.note: Opposing shareholders should get a buyback right. Her premise: a majority can impose losses on a minority.
steps.highlight: a majority can impose losses on a minority

steps.label: Dov's response
steps.note: He rejects the buyback right. But he concedes the harm. Concessions are agreement points.
steps.highlight: A minority can certainly be harmed by a majority's decision

steps.label: Predict the overlap
steps.note: Both say a majority's decision can harm a minority. They differ on what to do about it.

steps.label: Two-speaker check
steps.note: A: Dov yes, Imani silent. D: Dov yes, Imani no. E: Imani yes, Dov no. B and C both say harm, so compare them.

steps.label: Kill the near-twin
steps.note: B is nearly identical to C. The single word 'whenever' kills it: both speakers say harm can happen, and neither says it always does.

why.A: Only Dov says this. Imani takes no position on how boards would react.
why.B: Nearly the key, but 'whenever' kills it. Both speakers say harm can occur; neither says it always does.
why.C: Correct. Imani says a majority can impose losses on a minority, and Dov concedes a minority can be harmed by a majority's decision.
why.D: Dov implies it. Imani says a minority 'has no other way out', so she would deny it.
why.E: Imani says yes; Dov says no. That is a point of disagreement, not agreement.

slides.title: Cheat card
lines: Both speakers must take a position on the claim.
Agreement: both yes; look at what the second speaker concedes.
A topic only one speaker raises is never the answer.
